summary: This informational memo addresses the problems of extending the MARS multicast model across multiple clusters or subnets. It describes a hypothetical service called VENUS and shows how complex it would be.

eli5.summary: A thought experiment showing how hard it would be to run one mailing list across several towns.

questions: why is multicast harder to optimize across networks than unicast
why does multicast shortcutting cause control message explosion
what did venus teach us about multicast design
subtitle: Why extending multicast across multiple networks is vastly more complex than unicast.

tldr.problem: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) provides multicast over ATM within a single cluster or subnet. Some people wanted a multicast equivalent to NHRP, a unicast shortcut protocol that bypasses routers between subnets.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes VENUS (Very Extensive Non-Unicast Service), a hypothetical protocol exploring what such a system would need. It shows the coordination and scalability challenges: tracking group members across clusters, managing multiple independent MARS servers, and handling the explosion of control messages.
tldr.outcome: VENUS reveals why extending multicast shortcuts across multiple clusters is not straightforward. The complexity suggests that single-cluster MARS or pure multicast routing through routers may be simpler and better in practice.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Hypothetical multicast extension across multiple MARS clusters

facts.label: Key scalability issue
facts.value: Control message explosion: all MARS_JOIN and MARS_LEAVE from all clusters must be propagated everywhere

facts.label: Primary advantage lost
facts.value: Multicast router aggregation: a single Mrouter can represent many sources and many member changes

facts.label: Conclusion
facts.value: Complexity suggests simpler approaches (single cluster or routing through Mrouters) may be preferable

today: RFC 2191 is an informational RFC that was never standardized. It served as an exploration of why certain multicast shortcut ideas are intractable, informing later work on inter-cluster multicast. The thought experiment successfully convinced the community that certain naive approaches to multicast shortcuts do not scale.

sections.title: Multicast Shortcuts: Why It Is Harder Than Unicast
sections.content:
In regular unicast routing, the data path is point-to-point: one source sends to one destination. NHRP allows a source to discover a direct path to a destination and bypass intermediate routers, saving bandwidth and latency.

Multicast is different. In multicast, one source sends to many destinations that may be scattered across many subnets. Traditional multicast routing uses multicast routers (Mrouters) at the edges of subnets to aggregate traffic. A single Mrouter can represent 100 sources sending to a group, hiding individual flows. If sources try to bypass the Mrouter by sending directly to group members in other clusters, the Mrouters lose the ability to aggregate and optimize. The control plane also explodes: sources must now track every individual group member across every cluster, not just the Mrouters.
sections.eli5: With one person calling another, you can find a shortcut. But with one person broadcasting to many, telling every broadcast station what every listener wants gets impossibly complicated.

sections.title: The MARS Model and a VENUS Domain
sections.content:
MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) works within a single cluster, which is typically one subnet. A MARS server tracks all group members in its cluster. When a source wants to send to a multicast group, it queries its MARS, which returns the ATM addresses of all current group members. The source then sets up point-to-multipoint SVCs (Switched Virtual Circuits) to each member.

A VENUS Domain would span multiple MARS clusters. For this to work, each MARS would need to know about group members in all participating clusters, not just its own. When any host joins or leaves a multicast group anywhere in the domain, all the MARS servers must be told, and all sources must be kept up to date. A VENUS Domain looks very much like a single, huge distributed MARS Cluster.
sections.eli5: One post office handling subscriptions for one town works fine. But multiple post offices trying to coordinate subscriptions across all towns is like having to tell every single post office every time anyone anywhere subscribes or unsubscribes.

sections.title: The Group Member Discovery Problem
sections.content:
When a source in a VENUS Domain wants to send to a multicast group, it needs to know which group members are reachable. In a single MARS cluster, the MARS server has all the answers. Across multiple clusters, a MARS_REQUEST must somehow find all members wherever they are.

The RFC notes several complications. First, there is no single "right" path to query—members can be anywhere, so requests must be flooded or propagated along the multicast tree. Second, MARS clients have limits on how many leaf nodes (group members) they can handle. If a client can handle only 1000 members but the domain has 5000, the protocol must decide whether to return only the closest 1000 or to summarize distant clusters by their multicast router. Each choice affects where traffic flows and what optimizations are possible.

Third, if some clusters use Multicast Servers (MCS) instead of direct SVC meshes for a group, the VENUS discovery process must return the MCS address, not individual member addresses, to respect that cluster's local choice.
sections.eli5: Finding all the subscribers across multiple towns is tricky: do you ask everywhere? Just nearby towns? And if one town is too big, do you just give back the town's main address instead of every house address?

sections.title: The Control Message Explosion
sections.content:
Once a source has set up SVCs to group members, it must be kept informed of membership changes. In a single MARS cluster, MARS_JOIN and MARS_LEAVE messages are broadcast to the cluster's hosts and routers. Across a VENUS Domain, every MARS_JOIN and MARS_LEAVE from every cluster must be propagated to every potential source everywhere, because any host in any cluster could be a source for any group.

The RFC emphasizes the consequence: the signaling load is not localized. Instead of one MARS telling one cluster about membership changes, every MARS must tell every other MARS about every join and leave. This is "a larger scale version" of the already high broadcast load within a single cluster. The document notes that controlling this signaling growth is non-trivial, especially when different MARS Clients have different capacity limits and different portions of the VENUS Domain may have different densities of group members.
sections.eli5: Every post office has to tell every other post office every time someone subscribes or unsubscribes, just in case that person might send something. The noise drowns out everything.

sections.title: Dynamic State and Scaling Limits
sections.content:
A VENUS Domain raises additional questions about dynamic behavior. If a multicast group was using point-to-point SVCs in one cluster but then a Multicast Server (MCS) is deployed, how do remote sources switch to using the MCS? They need a new message type with semantics like "drop these leaf nodes {x, y, z} and add leaf node {a}, but leave everything else alone."

The RFC also raises the question of density over time. If a source initially queries for group members and the density was low, but more members join later, should the source dynamically expand the SVC scope? Or if different sources in the domain have different leaf node limits, can they establish different shortcut SVCs to different subsets of group members, and will this break multicast routing algorithms that assume aggregation at cluster boundaries?

The RFC notes: "we're up against the question of why you'd bypass an Mrouter." Mrouters perform two key functions: they aggregate data flows (100 senders become 1 outgoing SVC) and they hide signaling activity. Multicast shortcuts lose both benefits.
sections.eli5: Over time, more subscribers join. Does the original shortcut expand? If different towns have different capacities, some sources might reach some towns directly and others through the post office—and that confuses the routing.

viz.caption: Multicast routing uses routers (Mrouters) to aggregate; shortcuts bypass that aggregation
